---
title: "MaxSPRT and calibrated surveillance"
subtitle: "Sequential testing that accounts for systematic error"
---

## The setting

Vaccine and drug safety surveillance does not wait for the data to be complete.
Data accrue over time, and the analysis is repeated at every look — weekly,
monthly — with the intention of signalling as soon as there is evidence of harm.
Testing repeatedly inflates the type I error unless the test is designed for it.

The **maximised sequential probability ratio test** [@kulldorff2011] is the
standard answer. At each look, compute

$$
\mathrm{LLR} \;=\; \log \frac{L(\hat\beta)}{L(\beta_0)} \;=\; \ell(\hat\beta) - \ell(\beta_0),
$$

the log ratio of the likelihood at its maximum to the likelihood at the null,
truncated to zero when $\hat\beta < \beta_0$ so the test is one-sided. Signal
the first time $\mathrm{LLR}$ exceeds a critical value $\mathrm{CV}$ chosen so
that

$$
\Pr\!\left(\max_{k}\ \mathrm{LLR}_k \;\ge\; \mathrm{CV} \;\middle|\; H_0\right) \;=\; \alpha
$$

across the whole sequence of looks. The maximum over looks is what makes this a
*family-wise* guarantee rather than a per-look one.

And it is a guarantee about random error only. Surveillance runs on the same
observational data as everything else, with the same confounding, so the real
type I error is nothing like $\alpha$. There are two independent places to fix
that, and this package implements both.

## Fix 1: calibrate the statistic

Rather than comparing the observed LLR to a null at exactly $\beta_0$, compare
it to the **empirical null** — averaging the evidence over the plausible true
effects the design's systematic error could be manufacturing.

The route runs through p-values, because they are what averages sensibly. For a
one-sided test, Wilks' theorem gives $2\,\mathrm{LLR} \sim \chi^2_1$ under the
null, halved for one-sidedness:

$$
p \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\left(1 - F_{\chi^2_1}\!\left(2\,\mathrm{LLR}\right)\right),
\qquad
\mathrm{LLR} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} F^{-1}_{\chi^2_1}\!\left(1 - 2p\right).
$$

These are `computePFromLlr` and `computeLlrFromP`, and they are exact inverses.
Both switch to log-linear extrapolation in the extreme tail, where the $\chi^2$
routines return exactly 0 or $\infty$ — above $\mathrm{LLR} = 33$ and below
$p = 10^{-16}$ respectively.

With that bridge, the calibrated statistic is:

::: {.keyresult}
$$
p_{\text{cal}} \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
p\Big(\ell(\hat\beta) - \ell(x)\Big)\ \phi(x; \mu, \sigma)\ dx,
\qquad
\mathrm{LLR}_{\text{cal}} \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2} F^{-1}_{\chi^2_1}\!\left(1 - 2\,p_{\text{cal}}\right).
$$
:::

Read the integral as: for each candidate true effect $x$ that the empirical null
says the systematic error could be producing, compute the p-value you would get
if $x$ were the truth, and average those weighted by how plausible $x$ is.
`calibrateLlr` evaluates it numerically over $\mu \pm 10\sigma$. When
$\sigma < 0.001$ the integral degenerates and the LLR at $x = \mu$ is returned
directly.

```{python}
import empiricalcalibration as ec

sccs = ec.datasets.sccs()
negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
positive = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 1]

null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
llr_cal = ec.calibrateLlr(null, positive)
print("calibrated LLR:", llr_cal[0])
```

The calibrated LLR is zero: once the design's systematic error is accounted for,
this estimate carries no evidence against the null at all. The uncalibrated
statistic would have been large.

`calibrateLlr` accepts the same [likelihood
approximations](likelihood-approximations.qmd) as `fitNullNonNormalLl` — normal,
custom, skew-normal or grid — which matters here because surveillance signals
on small event counts where the normal approximation is poorest. It also accepts
an `McmcNull`, returning `llr`, `ci95Lb` and `ci95Ub`.

## Fix 2: calibrate the threshold

The other lever is the critical value. Instead of computing CV under a null that
assumes no systematic error, simulate under the **empirical** null: every
simulated trial draws its own systematic error $\exp(N(\mu, \sigma^2))$ and
applies it as a multiplier on the expected event counts. The resulting CV is
larger, and it delivers the nominal $\alpha$ against the error the design
actually has.

The three functions differ in the data-generating model:

| Function | Model | Key argument |
|---|---|---|
| `computeCvPoisson` | Poisson counts against a historical comparator | `groupSizes` = expected events under $H_0$ |
| `computeCvBinomial` | Binomial, self-controlled or matched | `z` = control-to-case ratio, so $p = 1/(1+z)$ |
| `computeCvPoissonRegression` | Poisson regression with a control window | `z` = control time / time at risk |

All three are Monte Carlo: simulate `sampleSize` trials under the null, record
the running maximum LLR across looks in each, and take the appropriate quantile.

```{python}
#| warning: false
# Ten monthly looks, one expected event per month under the null.
groupSizes = [1.0] * 10

ec.set_seed(1)
cv_plain = ec.computeCvPoisson(groupSizes, sampleSize=10_000)

ec.set_seed(1)
cv_calibrated = ec.computeCvPoisson(groupSizes, sampleSize=10_000,
                                    nullMean=null[0], nullSd=null[1])

print(f"CV, no systematic error:   {float(cv_plain):.3f}  (alpha {cv_plain.alpha})")
print(f"CV, empirical null:        {float(cv_calibrated):.3f}  (alpha {cv_calibrated.alpha})")
```

The threshold has to move a long way to hold the error rate against a design
this biased. If you were running surveillance with the uncalibrated CV, you were
operating at a far higher false-signal rate than the nominal 5%.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why `alpha` comes back different from what you asked for

With a discrete number of Monte-Carlo samples there is generally no critical
value achieving exactly $\alpha$. These functions choose the **least
conservative** CV whose realised alpha is still below the requested one, and
report what they achieved in `cv.alpha`. Always read it — with a small
`sampleSize` the gap can be substantial.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## These are the slow functions

The default `sampleSize=1_000_000` takes several seconds to tens of seconds per
call, against well under a second for the R package's C++. A vectorised path
handles the common regime (every Poisson mean below 10, every binomial $np$
below 30) and falls back to an exact scalar loop otherwise, so the answer is
identical either way. Drop `sampleSize` for exploration; keep the default for
anything you report, since the Monte-Carlo error in the CV is itself part of
your error budget.
:::

## Putting both together

A fully calibrated surveillance analysis uses both fixes: the calibrated LLR as
the statistic, and a CV simulated under the empirical null as the threshold.
`simulateMaxSprtData` generates a realistic multi-look dataset with negative and
positive controls for developing and testing such a pipeline.

```{python}
ec.set_seed(42)
data = ec.simulateMaxSprtData(n=1000, numberOfNegativeControls=5,
                              numberOfPositiveControls=1)
data.head()
```

Each row is a subject-outcome record; `lookTime` marks which sequential look it
belongs to and `outcomeId` which control. The
[MaxSPRT guide](../guide/maxsprt.qmd) works an analysis through end to end.

## API

| Function | Use |
|---|---|
| [`calibrateLlr(null, likelihoodApproximation)`](../reference/index.qmd#calibratellr) | Calibrated one-sided upper LLR. |
| [`computeCvPoisson(groupSizes, ...)`](../reference/index.qmd#computecvpoisson) | Critical value, Poisson design. |
| [`computeCvBinomial(groupSizes, z, ...)`](../reference/index.qmd#computecvbinomial) | Critical value, binomial design. |
| [`computeCvPoissonRegression(groupSizes, z, ...)`](../reference/index.qmd#computecvpoissonregression) | Critical value, Poisson regression design. |
| [`simulateMaxSprtData(...)`](../reference/index.qmd#simulatemaxsprtdata) | Simulated sequential surveillance data. |

Only one-sided upper LLRs are supported; `twoSided=True` or `upper=False` raise
`ValueError`, matching the R package.
